# ABSTRACT

Ausems, A. N. M. A., & Jensen, J.-K. (2026). {{< meta paper-title >}}. *Marine Ornithology*, 54(x), xxx–xxx. http://doi.org/10.5038/2074-1235.54.x.xxxx

Ongoing climate change and increasing human-induced environmental change are causing substantial declines in seabirds. The Atlantic Puffin *Fratercula arctica* (hereafter puffin) is one such species, experiencing declines across its North Atlantic range. While much of the declines in puffins are indirect, for example due to reduced food availability causing large-scale breeding failure, direct threats such as hunting may push already struggling populations over the edge. At the same time, samples from harvested puffins provide a unique opportunity to dissect and analyse a healthy segment of the population. Here, we analysed 13 yr (1995–2008) of data on female puffins harvested in *Føroyar* (Eng. the Faroe Islands) to determine whether the proportion of confirmed breeders (i.e., those females with 'convoluted' oviducts, indicating that they had laid an egg at least once in their lifetime) in the harvested sample increased over time. We also scored brood patch presence as a proxy for ongoing breeding in the sample year, as the harvest was carried out well into the chick rearing period and hormonal brood patches (without active breeding attempt) should have disappeared. We found that the observed proportion of confirmed breeders increased from approximately 15% in the earlier study years to 78% in 2008, and that within birds without brood patches, the proportion of confirmed breeders increased as well. Together, we showed that the representation of young, pre-breeding female birds declined in the sample, suggesting a substantial decline in recruitment. While the hunt is unlikely to be the main driver of the population decline in *Føroyar*, even reduced harvesting is likely unsustainable under current global conditions.

# SAMANDRÁTTUR

Áhaldandi veðurlagsbroytingar og øktar umhvørvisbroytingar av menniskjaávum hava við sær týðiligar broytingar í talinum á sjófugli. Eitt av ávirkaðu fuglasløgunum er lundin *Fratercula arctica*, sum er í minking í Norðuratlantshavi. Samstundis sum ein stórur partur av minkingini kemur av óbeinleiðis ávirkan, til dømis tí at minni føði hevur við sær, at stórur partur av ynglingini fer fyri skeytið, kunnu beinleiðis hóttanir, herundir lundaveiða, geva teimum longu hóttu lundastovnunum banahøggið. Fleygaðir lundar geva okkum eitt einastandandi høvi at kanna ein sunnan part av lundastovninum bæði inn- og útvortis. Her hava vit kannað 13 ára dátur (1995–2008) um lundabøgur, sum vórðu fleygaðar í Føroyum, við tí fyri eyga at vita, um lutfallið av váttaðum ynglifugl (t.e. tær lundabøgurnar, sum hava úttambaðar eggjaleiðarar, sum vísa, at tær hava vorpið í minsta lagi eina ferð) í kannaðu sýnunum øktist yvir tíð. Vit taldu eisini upp bølingarblettir sum tekin um yngling í kanningarárinum, av tí at sýnini vórðu tikin, eftir at eggini vóru klakt, og tá eiga hormonellir bølingarblettir (uttan virkna yngliroynd) at vera horvnir. Vit komu fram til, at lutfallið av váttaðum ynglifugli øktist frá umleið 15 % í byrjanini av kannaða tíðarskeiðinum til 78 % í 2008, og at lutfallið av váttaðum ynglifugli eisini øktist millum teir fuglarnar, sum ikki høvdu bølingarblett. Yvirhøvur kundu vit í sýnunum vísa á eina lækking av talinum á ungfuglum, sum ikki høvdu ynglað enn, og hetta bendir á stórar trupulleikar hjá stovninum at seta nýggjan ynglifugl við. Tað er neyvan veiðan, sum er høvuðsorsøkin til, at stovnurin minkar í Føroyum, men sjálvt avmarkað veiða er óburðardygg, soleiðis sum støðan er í dag hjá lundanum um allan heim.

**Key words:** demographics, seabirds, traditional harvest, recruitment, brood patch, seabird conservation

# INTRODUCTION

Global climate change and increasing human-induced environmental change are causing large-scale declines in many seabird species [@diasThreatsSeabirdsGlobal2019]. Some threats have indirect effects, for example, climate change may cause a decline in food availability leading to lower breeding success, and eventually observable population declines [@fayetLocalPreyShortages2021]. On the other hand, other threats directly cause mortality, such as bycatch, hunting and increased storms due to climate change [@clairbauxNorthAtlanticWinter2021]. In long-lived species such as seabirds, changes in adult survival can have strong effects on population dynamics [@jenouvrierModellingPopulationDynamics2005a; @dohertyTestingLifeHistory2004]. Even minor threats directly affecting survival can have large impacts, which may have especially detrimental effects in already vulnerable species where small or declining populations can absorb less additional mortality. In contrast, the elasticity of population growth rate to breeding success and recruitment rate is relatively low, but because they can react strongly to changes in environmental conditions [@jenouvrierModellingPopulationDynamics2005a], these factors may have the strongest effect on population growth rate overall [@milesDeclineAtlanticPuffin2015]. In fact, birds of pre-breeding age can make up more than half the population size, and their disappearance can have strong impacts on population health [@taylorPrebreedingPopulationsImportance2026].

Atlantic Puffins *Fratercula arctica* (hereafter 'puffin') are rapidly declining across most of their European range [@birdlifeinternationalSpeciesFactsheetFratercula2021], and they are classified as ‘Vulnerable’ globally and ‘Endangered’ in Europe [@birdlifeinternationalFraterculaArcticaIUCN2018]. Puffin population declines are largely linked to changes in food availability causing declines in breeding success [@fayetLocalPreyShortages2021] and thus recruitment rate leading to increases in the age of the population [@ausemsVariationFoodAvailability2026]. On average, puffins start breeding when they are between 4 and 5 yr old, occasionally they can start as early as 3 yr old, and often the first breeding attempt is after 5 yr old [@lowtherAtlanticPuffinFratercula2020]. Annual survival of both immatures and adults is high [@sandvikHighSurvivalImmatures2008], though immature survival may vary between sites and years [see @ashcroftSurvivalRatesBreeding1979], and immatures are highly philopatric [@sandvikHighSurvivalImmatures2008].

In *Føroyar* (Eng. Faroe Islands; @fig-map), harvesting puffins is a long-standing, culturally important tradition, where hunters catch flying puffins from set locations on land using a specially made net. Puffins are a widespread species in the islands, with an estimated 550,000 breeding pairs in approximately 100 colonies [@jensenListBirdsSeen2005; @hammerFaeroskTraekfugleatlasFaroese2014]. However, as in other areas, their population shows observed, but unquantified, declines in *Føroyar*. Overharvesting has long been understood to negatively affect the local population [@jensenTraditionsPuffinFowling2020], and, on Nólsoy (@fig-map), the harvest was voluntarily halted in 2009 until the population was deemed stable enough in 2021 to sustain limited harvesting [@ausemsVariationFoodAvailability2026]. As with the assessment of the decline, this status change was not based on rigorous counts, but rather a general impression of the colony, and may thus be subject to shifting baselines [@paulyAnecdotesShiftingBaseline1995; @saenz-arroyoRapidlyShiftingEnvironmental2005; @papworthEvidenceShiftingBaseline2009].

Puffin hunters, or fowlers, follow a set of rules intended to ensure only young, prospecting birds are caught and catching breeding adults is avoided [@jensenPuffinFowlingaFowling2010]. Puffin harvesting is restricted to the chick-rearing period as this makes it easier to distinguish breeding adults and prospecting juveniles [@jensenPuffinFowlingaFowling2010]. During the breeding season, puffins take part in 'wheeling-flight', where large groups of birds fly in circles or figure-8s over the colony and surrounding water [@lowtherAtlanticPuffinFratercula2020]. It is assumed that only prospecting birds take part in this behaviour, while breeding adults will either be identifiable by them carrying fish to their nest or directly heading back to sea to collect more food for the chick [@jensenPuffinFowlingaFowling2010]. Puffins do not necessarily display this behaviour every day; rather they come to the colony on specific *landkomudagar* (literally translated "land-coming days", i.e., days when a large number of birds attend the colony; historically mostly young puffins, but in struggling colonies often adults that skipped breeding or failed breeders, J-KJ, pers. obs.) when weather conditions are favourable, which are the preferred hunting days. Hunters only trap birds taking part in the wheeling-flight behaviour. In addition, if a bird with wet bill and cheeks is caught, it is released again, as that is a sign of a bird having just delivered fish to its young.

Ongoing global climate change and anthropogenic impacts have altered puffin breeding phenology and propensity. In northern latitudes, puffins are breeding later [@burrLaterHigherLatitudes2016] in response to environmental conditions [@durantRegimeShiftsBreeding2004; @majorContrastingPhenologicalDemographic2021]. Furthermore, birds are forced to forage further offshore to find sufficient food, leading to increases in breeding failures [@fayetLocalPreyShortages2021]. Together, these changes may affect the efficacy of self-imposed rules; non-incubating partners and failed breeders may take part in the 'wheeling-flight' behaviour without showing the tell-tale signs of being of breeding age.

Using a 20-yr dataset on legally harvested puffins [@fuglaveiduloginLogtingslogUmFuglaveidu1984], we tested whether females of breeding age were harvested. We hypothesise that, as the overall age of the population is increasing and the proportion of young (i.e., \<4 calendar yr) is declining [@ausemsVariationFoodAvailability2026], the proportion of females of breeding age in the sample increased over the study period. Secondly, we tested whether breeding propensity changed over time by assessing brood patch presence in the sample. We could not find studies detailing the development and regression of brood patches in puffins or other auks, but in other birds, brood patch formation is induced by hormones before the breeding season [@jonesIncubationPatchBirds1971] and it quickly disappears when a bird is not incubating an egg [@baileyIncubationPatchPasserine1952]. While brood patch presence might be a misleading sign of breeding status [@tranquillaReliabilityBroodPatches2003], we assumed that, at the time of the puffin hunt, prospecting and failed breeders would have refeathered their brood patches as their hormone levels went back down, while actively incubating and brooding birds still retained theirs. We predicted that females of breeding age would be less likely to have brood patches later in the study period, indicating increased breeding failures or an increase in birds foregoing breeding.

# Methods

```{r data}
harvest <- read_csv("../data/harvest.csv") |>
  select(-Notes) |> 
  filter(Year < 2009)

data_all <- read_rds("../data/data.rds")

# dates as "02 July" (MO style), with English month names regardless of locale.
# Dates listed in dates_to_check are printed bold red in the Word output so they
# are easy to find for checking; empty the vector (as.Date(character(0))) once
# they are confirmed or corrected.
dates_to_check <- as.Date(character(0))

# negative numbers in the text with a proper minus sign (U+2212), not a hyphen
fmt_minus <- function(x) sub("^-", "−", as.character(x))

fmt_day_month <- function(x) {
  txt <- paste(format(x, "%d"), month.name[as.integer(format(x, "%m"))])
  flag <- as.Date(x) %in% dates_to_check
  txt[flag] <- paste0("`<w:r><w:rPr><w:b/><w:color w:val=\"FF0000\"/></w:rPr>",
                      "<w:t xml:space=\"preserve\">", txt[flag], "</w:t></w:r>`{=openxml}")
  txt
}

# records with a reliable sampling date, for the date ranges in the Methods and
# tbl-harvest only: excludes dates flagged in the data as uncertain (08 June
# 2006, a confirmed data-entry error with unknown true date; two Sundays, which
# lie within their year's range anyway). All records stay in the analysis,
# which uses year only (see scripts/flag_uncertain_dates.R)
data_dated <- data_all |> filter(!date_uncertain)

# earliest and latest calendar day sampled in any year (by day of the season,
# ignoring the year), for the Methods
season_day   <- format(data_dated$date, "%m-%d")
date_earliest <- data_dated$date[order(season_day)][1]
date_latest   <- data_dated$date[order(season_day, decreasing = TRUE)][1]

# year(s) in which a calendar day was sampled: the year if only one, otherwise
# "several years" (the years are listed in tbl-harvest)
which_years <- function(x) {
  yrs <- unique(data_dated$year[season_day == format(x, "%m-%d")])
  if (length(yrs) == 1) as.character(yrs) else "several years"
}

females <- data_all |>
  filter(sex == "Female") |>
  filter_out(is.na(bred)) |>
  select(date, brood.spot, bred, year) |>
  mutate(year_c = (year - mean(year)) / 10) |> # decades from mean year, for interpretable logit-scale priors
  drop_na(brood.spot)

harvest <- harvest |>
  left_join(
    females |>
      group_by(year) |>
      summarise(Females = n(),
                `% Bred (*n*)` = sprintf("%.0f%% (%d)", mean(bred) * 100, sum(bred)),
                .groups = "drop"),
    by = join_by(Year == year))
```

Ethics statement: all birds were legally harvested [@fuglaveiduloginLogtingslogUmFuglaveidu1984], and none of the birds were killed on request specially for this study.

Between 1989 and 2008, J-KJ inspected `r format(nrow(data_all), big.mark = ",")` haphazardly selected puffins harvested on the islands of Nólsoy from 1989 to 2006, and on Mykines in 2007 and 2008 (@tbl-harvest), when no puffins could be obtained on Nólsoy (@fig-map). The puffin harvest officially opens 02 July, with an end-date of 08 August. Sampling never started before 02 July (@tbl-harvest), but the end date was not always adhered to as the latest sample in our dataset was harvested `r fmt_day_month(date_latest)` (`r which_years(date_latest)`; @tbl-harvest). J-KJ acquired an arbitrary number of puffins (range: `r paste(round(range(harvest[[3]], na.rm = TRUE), 1), collapse = "–")`; median: `r round(median(harvest[[3]], na.rm = TRUE), 1)`; @tbl-harvest) from hunters when they returned to the village. Hunters placed the harvested puffins in a big pile on the ground prior to processing. From one pile per hunting day, J-KJ collected a haphazard sample by closing his eyes when selecting birds. The estimated number of harvested puffins between 1996 and 2008 ranged from `r format(min(harvest[[2]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` (`r harvest$Year[which.min(harvest[[2]])]`) to `r format(max(harvest[[2]], na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` (`r harvest$Year[which.max(harvest[[2]])]`; @tbl-harvest) but similar counts do not exist for the period between 1989 and 1995.

J-KJ scored the presence or absence of brood patches before dissecting all individuals to determine their sex starting in 1995. For females, J-KJ determined whether they had ever laid an egg by assessing the oviduct; a straight oviduct indicates that a female never laid an egg, while a 'convoluted' oviduct indicates that a female has laid an egg and therefore is of confirmed breeding age [@vanfraneker2004]. For males, it is impossible to determine whether they have bred before. Based on bill characteristics, we could only determine their age up to 4 yr [@ausemsVariationFoodAvailability2026] which is generally too young to be of breeding age [@lowtherAtlanticPuffinFratercula2020]. Therefore, we only included females for which their breeding status could be determined in our analyses (*n* = `r format(nrow(females), big.mark = ",")`). We removed individuals for which breeding state could not be determined (*n* = `r data_all |> filter(sex == "Female") |> filter(year > 1994) |> filter(is.na(bred)) |> tally() |> pull(n)`) and individuals for which the presence of brood patches was not scored (*n* = `r data_all |> filter(sex == "Female") |> filter(year > 1994) |> filter(is.na(brood.spot)) |> tally()`).

We fitted a Bayesian generalised linear model (GLM) with logistic regression \[logit link, Bernoulli family; function *brm*, package *brms* version `r packageVersion("brms")`; @burknerBrmsPackageBayesian2017\] in R \[version `r getRversion()`; @rcoreteamLanguageEnvironmentStatistical2026a\] with breeding status (0 = never bred; 1 = has bred) as response variable. We included study year and brood patch presence (0 = absent; 1 = present) with an interaction as covariates. We used weakly informative priors: a normal (0, 1.5) prior on the brood patch presence and year × brood patch presence interaction, a more sceptical normal (0, 1) prior on the year trend, and the default Student-*t* (3, 0, 2.5) prior on the intercept. We centred year around the mean, and scaled it in decades, so the year prior constrains the plausible per-decade change in breeding probability. We confirmed that these priors implied plausible values using prior predictive checks [*pp_check* with *type = "stat"* and *stat = "mean"*; @burknerBrmsPackageBayesian2017], before fitting the model to the data. We ran six chains, each with 4,000 iterations of which 2,000 were discarded as warmup, and without thinning. We report all estimates as posterior medians with 95% credible intervals (CI; 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the posterior).

We assessed Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) convergence by inspecting trace plots for all parameters [@gabryVisualizationBayesianWorkflow2019], confirming that $\hat{R}$ values were close to 1 [≤ 1.01; @vehtariRankNormalizationFoldingLocalization2021], and that effective sample sizes (bulk/tail ESS) were high for all fixed effects [i.e., \> 100 per chain; @vehtariRankNormalizationFoldingLocalization2021]. We evaluated posterior predictive fit graphically using *pp_check* [@burknerBrmsPackageBayesian2017], comparing the observed distribution of breeding status to the posterior predictive distribution [@gelmanPosteriorPredictiveAssessment1996; @gabryVisualizationBayesianWorkflow2019]. We assessed out-of-sample predictive performance using approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO) assuming a good fit if the Pareto *k* value was \< 0.7 for all observations [function *loo*; @burknerBrmsPackageBayesian2017; @vehtariPracticalBayesianModel2017; @vehtariParetoSmoothedImportance2024].

As a robustness check, we tested whether brood patch detectability drifted over time within females of confirmed breeding age with a second GLM with brood patch presence as response variable and year as covariate, including only females of confirmed breeding age (*n* = `r females |> filter(bred == 1) |> drop_na(brood.spot) |> tally() |> pull(n) |> format(big.mark = ",")`). We used the same priors as for the full model, excluding the interaction term. As a second robustness check to confirm that the low sample size (*n* = `r harvest |> filter(Year == 2007) |> pull(Females)`) in 2007 did not have an undue effect on the overall outcome, we refit the full model excluding 2007. We also tested whether the change in sampling location had an effect by refitting the model excluding individuals collected on Mykines.

```{r model-fit}
#| include: false

priors <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b"), # slopes, incl. brood.spot and interaction
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", coef = "year_c"), # skeptical prior on the trend
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 2.5), class = "Intercept")
)

# prior predictive check before trusting the priors above
m01_prior <- brm(bred ~ year_c * brood.spot,
                 data = females,
                 family = bernoulli(),
                 prior = priors,
                 file = "../output/priors.rds",
                 file_refit = "on_change",,
                 sample_prior = "only")

pp_prior <- pp_check(m01_prior, type = "stat", stat = "mean")
ggsave("../figures/prior_pred_check.png", pp_prior, dpi = 500)

m01 <- brm(bred ~ year_c * brood.spot,
           data = females,
           family = bernoulli(),
           prior = priors,
           seed = 42,
           iter = 4000,
           cores = parallel::detectCores() - 1,
           chains = 6,
           sample_prior = "yes",
           file = "../output/m01.rds",
           file_refit = "on_change",
           silent = 2,
           save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE))

summary(m01)
pp_model <- pp_check(m01, type = "stat", stat = "mean")
ggsave("../figures/model_pred_check.png", pp_model, dpi = 500)

loo_m1 <- loo(m01)

mcmc_dat <- bayesplot::mcmc_trace_data(m01)
mcmc_model <- bayesplot::mcmc_trace(m01)
ggsave("../figures/mcmc_plot.png", mcmc_model, dpi = 500)
```

```{r robustness-check1}
#| include: false

breeders <- females |> 
  filter(bred == 1) |> 
  drop_na(brood.spot)

priors2 <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", coef = "year_c"),
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 2.5), class = "Intercept")
)

m02 <- brm(brood.spot ~ year_c,
           data = breeders,
           family = bernoulli(),
           prior = priors2,
           seed = 42,
           iter = 4000,
           cores = parallel::detectCores() - 1,
           chains = 6,
           sample_prior = "yes",
           file = "../output/m02.rds",
           file_refit = "on_change",
           silent = 2,
           save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE))

summary(m02)
pp_model2 <- pp_check(m02, type = "stat", stat = "mean")
ggsave("../figures/model2_pred_check.png", pp_model2, dpi = 500)

loo_m2 <- loo(m02)

mcmc_dat2 <- bayesplot::mcmc_trace_data(m02)
mcmc_model2 <- bayesplot::mcmc_trace(m02)
ggsave("../figures/mcmc_plot2.png", mcmc_model2, dpi = 500)
```

```{r robustness-check3}
#| include: false

# Nólsoy only: all Mykines samples are from 2007 and 2008 (and those years are
# Mykines only), and the data have no site column, so filter on year. year_c
# keeps the full-data centring so coefficients are comparable with m01.
females_nolsoy <- females |> filter(!year %in% c(2007, 2008))

m01_sens_mykines <- brm(bred ~ year_c * brood.spot,
```

# Results

The model passed the validation checks (Appendix) with all $\hat{R}$ ≤ 1.001 and high ESS (bulk/tail ESS \> 8,900 of 12,000 post-warmup draws). All Pareto *k* estimates were \< 0.7 (expected log pointwise predictive density \[ELPD\] ± standard error \[SE\] = `r fmt_minus(round(loo_m1[[1]][[1]], 2))` ± `r round(loo_m1[[1]][[4]], 2)`, effective parameters ± SE = `r round(loo_m1[[1]][[2]], 2)` ± `r round(loo_m1[[1]][[5]], 2)`). The robustness check models also passed all checks (Appendix).

```{r pop-trend}
# population-averaged (standardised) change in P(bred) across the study period,
# integrating over the observed brood.spot mix -- stays within the observed year_c
# range, unlike a naive per-decade extrapolation of the year_c coefficient
yr_min <- min(females$year_c)
yr_max <- max(females$year_c)

nd_start <- females |> mutate(year_c = yr_min)
nd_end   <- females |> mutate(year_c = yr_max)

avg_start <- rowMeans(posterior_epred(m01, newdata = nd_start))
avg_end   <- rowMeans(posterior_epred(m01, newdata = nd_end))
pop_trend_diff <- avg_end - avg_start

# first and last study year as observed, and as predicted for that year's own
# brood patch composition -- the same averaging as the line in fig-marg-bar
females_first <- females |> filter(year == min(year))
obs_first_n    <- nrow(females_first)
obs_first_bred <- sum(females_first$bred)
bp_first       <- mean(females_first$brood.spot)
pred_first     <- rowMeans(posterior_epred(m01, newdata = females_first))

females_last <- females |> filter(year == max(year))
obs_last_n    <- nrow(females_last)
obs_last_bred <- sum(females_last$bred)
bp_last       <- mean(females_last$brood.spot)
bp_pooled     <- mean(females$brood.spot)
pred_last     <- rowMeans(posterior_epred(m01, newdata = females_last))

# odds ratios per decade, on the draw scale (posterior medians, which equal exp(fixef(robust = TRUE))
# used in tbl-odds-m1) -- computed directly rather than via hypothesis(), since
# hypothesis() reports the shifted quantity exp(year_c) - 1 for a one-sided test,
# not the odds ratio itself
m01_draws <- as_draws_df(m01)
or_baseline <- exp(m01_draws$b_year_c)
or_present  <- exp(m01_draws$b_year_c + m01_draws$`b_year_c:brood.spot`)

hyp_baseline <- hypothesis(m01, "year_c > 0")[[1]]
hyp_present  <- hypothesis(m01, "year_c + year_c:brood.spot > 0")[[1]]
```

```{r model2-interpret}
#| include: false

odds2 <- fixef(m02, robust = TRUE)[, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")] |>
  exp() |>
  round(2)

# one-sided test: did brood-spot presence decline over time among breeders?
hypothesis(m02, "year_c < 0")
```

```{r sens2007-interpret}
#| include: false

# per-coefficient odds ratios for m01 vs. the 2007-excluded refit, on the same
# median (robust = TRUE) convention as tbl-odds1, so the deltas are directly comparable
# to the numbers in that table
or_full <- exp(fixef(m01, robust = TRUE)[, "Estimate"])
or_sens <- exp(fixef(m01_sens2007, robust = TRUE)[, "Estimate"])
or_diff <- or_sens - or_full

# change for the text: negative values keep their minus sign, positive values
# get no "+", and anything that rounds to zero prints as "0.00" (not "-0.00")
fmt_delta <- function(x) {
  x <- round(x, 2)
  if (x == 0) "0.00" else fmt_minus(sprintf("%.2f", x))
}
```

```{r sens-mykines-interpret}
#| include: false

# same comparison for the Nólsoy-only refit (2007 and 2008 excluded), plus the
# per-decade odds ratios by brood patch group, as reported for the full model
or_sens_myk  <- exp(fixef(m01_sens_mykines, robust = TRUE)[, "Estimate"])
or_diff_myk  <- or_sens_myk - or_full

myk_draws         <- as_draws_df(m01_sens_mykines)
or_baseline_myk   <- exp(myk_draws$b_year_c)
or_present_myk    <- exp(myk_draws$b_year_c + myk_draws$`b_year_c:brood.spot`)
hyp_baseline_myk  <- hypothesis(m01_sens_mykines, "year_c > 0")[[1]]
hyp_present_myk   <- hypothesis(m01_sens_mykines, "year_c + year_c:brood.spot > 0")[[1]]
```

The GLM showed an increase in the proportion of females of confirmed breeding age over time (@fig-marg-bar), with a strong increase within females without brood patches, and a less certain increase in females with brood patches (@fig-pred1). In the first study year (`r min(females$year)`), `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * obs_first_bred / obs_first_n)`% (`r obs_first_bred` of `r obs_first_n`) of sampled females were of confirmed breeding age. Given that year's brood patch composition (`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * bp_first)`% with brood patches), the model predicted a probability of `r sprintf("%.2f", median(pred_first))` (95% CI: `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(pred_first, 0.025))`–`r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(pred_first, 0.975))`). In comparison, in the last year of the study period (`r max(females$year)`), `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * obs_last_bred / obs_last_n)`% (`r obs_last_bred` of `r obs_last_n`) of sampled females were of confirmed breeding age, an increase of `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * ((obs_last_bred / obs_last_n) - (obs_first_bred / obs_first_n)))` percentage points. Given that year's brood patch composition (`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * bp_last)`% with brood patches), the model predicted a probability of `r sprintf("%.2f", median(pred_last))` (95% CI: `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(pred_last, 0.025))`–`r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(pred_last, 0.975))`; @fig-marg-bar), an increase of `r sprintf("%.2f", median(pred_last)-median(pred_first))`. Standardised to the average brood patch composition across all years (`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * bp_pooled)`%), the predicted probability increased from `r sprintf("%.2f", median(avg_start))` (95% CI: `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(avg_start, 0.025))`–`r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(avg_start, 0.975))`) in `r min(females$year)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", median(avg_end))` (95% CI: `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(avg_end, 0.025))`–`r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(avg_end, 0.975))`) in `r max(females$year)`, an increase of `r sprintf("%.2f", median(pop_trend_diff))` (95% CI: `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(pop_trend_diff, 0.025))`–`r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(pop_trend_diff, 0.975))`) over the study period. Confirmed breeding odds increased by a factor of `r sprintf("%.2f", median(or_baseline))` (95% CI: `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(or_baseline, 0.025))`–`r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(or_baseline, 0.975))`; posterior probability of an increase = `r sprintf("%.1f", hyp_baseline$Post.Prob * 100)`%) per decade in females without brood patches (the baseline for the model) and `r sprintf("%.2f", median(or_present))` (95% CI: `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(or_present, 0.025))`–`r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(or_present, 0.975))`; posterior probability of an increase = `r sprintf("%.1f", hyp_present$Post.Prob * 100)`%) for females with brood patches (@tbl-odds1; @fig-pred1).

We found no credible trend in brood patch presence within females of confirmed breeding age (odds ratio `r sprintf("%.2f", odds2[[2]])`/decade; 95% CI \[`r sprintf("%.2f", odds2[[4]])`–`r sprintf("%.2f", odds2[[6]])`\]; posterior probability of a decrease = `r sprintf("%.1f", hypothesis(m02, "year_c < 0")[[1]]$Post.Prob * 100)`%; @fig-pred2).

Removing only 2007 did not change the model predictions (Δ odds ratio, 2007-excluded refit minus full model: intercept `r fmt_delta(or_diff[["Intercept"]])`, year `r fmt_delta(or_diff[["year_c"]])`, brood patch presence `r fmt_delta(or_diff[["brood.spot"]])`, interaction `r fmt_delta(or_diff[["year_c:brood.spot"]])`). Removing Mykines (i.e., 2007 and 2008) did not change the model conclusions, but reduced the effect (Δ odds ratio, Mykines-excluded refit minus full model: intercept `r fmt_delta(or_diff_myk[["Intercept"]])`, year `r fmt_delta(or_diff_myk[["year_c"]])`, brood patch presence `r fmt_delta(or_diff_myk[["brood.spot"]])`, interaction `r fmt_delta(or_diff_myk[["year_c:brood.spot"]])`). Without Mykines, confirmed breeding odds increased by a factor of `r sprintf("%.2f", median(or_baseline_myk))` (95% CI: `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(or_baseline_myk, 0.025))`–`r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(or_baseline_myk, 0.975))`; posterior probability of an increase = `r sprintf("%.1f", hyp_baseline_myk$Post.Prob * 100)`%) per decade in females without brood patches and `r sprintf("%.2f", median(or_present_myk))` (95% CI: `r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(or_present_myk, 0.025))`–`r sprintf("%.2f", quantile(or_present_myk, 0.975))`; posterior probability of an increase = `r sprintf("%.1f", hyp_present_myk$Post.Prob * 100)`%) for females with brood patches.

# Discussion

Our results show that the self-imposed rules were reasonably effective early in the study period when between 7% and 35% of the female harvest before 2005 were birds of confirmed breeding age (@tbl-harvest). However, in the later years leading up to the suspension of the harvest, the observed proportion of birds of confirmed breeding age steeply increased to a peak of 78% (@tbl-harvest). Our model showed that this increase was not an artefact of changes in brood patch prevalence. Standardised to a constant brood patch composition, the model-predicted probability of confirmed breeding more than tripled over the study period (@fig-marg-bar), and it increased in females without brood patches and, less certainly, in females with brood patches (@fig-pred1). This pattern held when excluding the Mykines samples, although the estimated increase was smaller (Appendix). Furthermore, we found no trend in brood patch presence among females of confirmed breeding age (@fig-pred2), indicating that 1) birds of breeding age were not more or less likely to attempt breeding in a given year, and 2) within the group of birds without brood patches, birds of breeding age became more prevalent (@fig-pred1). Together, this indicates that pre-breeding birds became less represented in the sample, rather than brood patch detectability changing in birds of confirmed breeding age.

While our previous work [@ausemsVariationFoodAvailability2026] showed a clear disappearance of the younger birds from the sample, we were not able to age individuals past 4 calendar yr. Our current study only includes female birds, as we cannot confirm breeding status in males [@vanfraneker2004]. Considering the strong pair bond and the fact that males tend to start breeding at a slightly earlier age [@ashcroftSurvivalRatesBreeding1979], we believe our results reflect the state of the entire population. Combined, both studies [this study and @ausemsVariationFoodAvailability2026] strongly suggest that recruitment rate is insufficient [@milesDeclineAtlanticPuffin2015], and young birds are disappearing.

Besides the absence of younger birds, older, breeding-age birds may be increasingly likely to be caught as breeding success decreases in much of the North Atlantic range [@milesDeclineAtlanticPuffin2015; @fayetLocalPreyShortages2021]. Failed breeders often remain in the area, joining the prospecting birds in the 'wheeling-flight' behaviour [@lowtherAtlanticPuffinFratercula2020], thus increasing the likelihood of being captured. With increased food shortages due to climate change and anthropogenic pressures [@fayetLocalPreyShortages2021], more breeding attempts fail. Secondly, puffin phenology is affected by environmental conditions [@durantRegimeShiftsBreeding2004], with puffins breeding later in more recent years [@majorContrastingPhenologicalDemographic2021]. Therefore, the hunting season may start to overlap with the incubation period, when the off-duty parent may join the 'wheeling-flight' behaviour, rather than purely the chick-rearing period when both parents are on duty.

Our study is based on data collected several decades ago, with the latest study year being 2008. As no comprehensive counts are collected in the Nólsoy colony, there is no evidence showing whether the trends are continuing or not. The fact that the colony was deemed stable enough to sustain (limited) harvesting in 2021 [@ausemsVariationFoodAvailability2026] suggests that the colony has substantially grown between 2008 and 2021. However, this status change was not based on counts but rather the impression of the hunters and may thus be subject to shifting baselines [@paulyAnecdotesShiftingBaseline1995; @papworthEvidenceShiftingBaseline2009; @saenz-arroyoRapidlyShiftingEnvironmental2005]. In fact, the decision was largely based on the absence of a 'disaster year' (i.e., years with no or exceptionally low breeding success, as observed from the absence of fledglings in the colony) since 2013, and it is likely an objective observer would not consider colony health to have improved between 2008 and 2021 [see the yearly breeding season descriptions in @jensenBreedingSeason2021, with links to earlier years]. Furthermore, @stempniewiczPuffinHarvestingSurvival2007 note that in the late 1990s, "10,000 individuals were taken annually at the Nólsoy colony", which likely exceeded the recruitment rate and population decline was probably only delayed by the immigration of immature puffins from elsewhere. Considering the reported global decline of Atlantic Puffins [@birdlifeinternationalFraterculaArcticaIUCN2018], we believe it likely that the Faroese population is affected by the same environmental drivers of this decrease.

Overall, we believe that the harvested sample, although intentionally biased towards younger birds, represents an ongoing trend in the whole Faroese, and potentially North Atlantic, population: insufficient recruitment that is causing the overall population to age [@milesDeclineAtlanticPuffin2015; @fayetLocalPreyShortages2021; @ausemsVariationFoodAvailability2026]. While we do not think the traditional harvest is the main driver behind the population collapse in *Føroyar*, as this is most likely caused by ongoing climate change and food shortages [@ausemsVariationFoodAvailability2026; @fayetLocalPreyShortages2021; @milesDeclineAtlanticPuffin2015], it may push an already struggling population over the edge [@johnsonRegionalDemographyIcelandic2024]. In fact, in Iceland, where a similar hunting tradition exists, even greatly reduced harvesting is deemed unsustainable in current conditions [@johnson2024icelandic]. In Scotland, the traditional *guga* (juvenile Northern Gannet *Morus bassanus*) hunting licence was rejected this year (2026) as the requested harvest was deemed likely to negatively affect the population [@naturescot2026guga].

```{r mod-marg-bar}
#| label: fig-marg-bar

females_cc <- females |> drop_na(brood.spot)
epred <- posterior_epred(m01, newdata = females_cc)  # draws x observations

yrs <- sort(unique(females_cc$year))
draws_by_year <- sapply(yrs, function(y) rowMeans(epred[, females_cc$year == y, drop = FALSE]))
colnames(draws_by_year) <- yrs

marginal_summary <- as_tibble(draws_by_year) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "year", values_to = "draw") |>
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(Estimate = median(draw), Q2.5 = quantile(draw, .025), Q97.5 = quantile(draw, .975), .groups = "drop")

observed_overall <- females_cc |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(prop_bred = mean(bred), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

puffin_pal <- seabird_palettes$atlanticpuffin

mod_marg_bar <- marginal_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year)) +
  geom_col(data = observed_overall, aes(y = prop_bred), fill = puffin_pal[5], alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q2.5, ymax = Q97.5), alpha = 0.15, fill = puffin_pal[5]) +

  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +

       y = "Probability of confirmed breeding")
```

```{r tbl-harvest}
             format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             align = "r",
```

```{r tbl-odds-m1}
#| label: tbl-odds1
#| tbl-cap: "Odds ratios for all fixed effects of the Bayesian generalised linear model testing temporal changes in the breeding status of Atlantic Puffins *Fratercula arctica* harvest in Føroyar (1995–2008)^a^"

knitr::kable(fixef(m01, robust = TRUE)[, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")] |>
  exp() |>
  round(2) |>
  `rownames<-`(c("Intercept", "Year (in decades)", "Brood patches (BP)", "Year: BP")),
  col.names = c("Estimate", "Lower 95% CI", "Upper 95% CI"))
```

::: {custom-style="footnote text"}
^a^ The model included breeding status (0 = never bred, 1 = has bred) as response variable, and year, brood patches (0 = absent, 1 = present), and their interaction as covariates.
:::
